learn.intro: A 'balance of terror' made direct war unthinkable, so rivalry moved into proxy conflicts. At the same time, the costs of Vietnam, the Sino-Soviet conflict and Soviet economic needs pushed the superpowers into détente — arms control, summits and the Helsinki Accords — until it unravelled at the end of the 1970s.

blocks.p: Brezhnev led the USSR from October 1964; Andrei Gromyko was Foreign Minister from 1957 to 1985, providing continuity. Nixon (President 1969–74) and Henry Kissinger (National Security Adviser, then Secretary of State) pursued realpolitik — dealing with rivals on the basis of interests, not ideology — and 'triangular diplomacy' between Moscow and Beijing. Mao, fearing the USSR after the 1969 border clashes, was willing to talk to the USA.

Summits and visits: Glassboro (1967, Johnson and Kosygin); Nixon's visit to China (February 1972); the Moscow Summit (May 1972), where SALT I and the Basic Principles agreement were signed; Brezhnev's visit to the USA (1973); Vladivostok (1974, Ford and Brezhnev); Vienna (June 1979, Carter and Brezhnev), where SALT II was signed.

The USSR expanded its navy under Admiral Gorshkov into a global force and rapidly increased its nuclear warheads and missiles, reaching rough parity with the USA by around 1970. The USA developed more sophisticated technology, such as MIRVs (several warheads on one missile, deployed from 1970) and anti-ballistic missile (ABM) systems.

MAD — Mutually Assured Destruction: each side could destroy the other even after being attacked first, so neither could win a nuclear war. This deterred direct conflict and encouraged arms control; the hot-line was upgraded in 1971.

The Middle East: the USA backed Israel and the USSR backed Egypt and Syria. In the Six-Day War (1967) and the Yom Kippur War (October 1973) the superpowers re-supplied their allies; in 1973 US forces were put on heightened alert when the USSR threatened to intervene.

Africa: in Angola (from 1975) the USSR and Cuban troops supported the MPLA while the USA and South Africa backed its rivals; in the Horn of Africa (1977–78) Soviet and Cuban support helped Ethiopia against Somalia. American critics saw these as Soviet exploitation of détente.

South and Central America: the US feared Marxist influence in its 'backyard'. It worked to undermine Salvador Allende's elected socialist government in Chile, which was overthrown in a military coup in September 1973. The Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua (1979) renewed American fears.

Reasons: the cost and unpopularity of the Vietnam War made the USA want to reduce commitments and enlist Soviet and Chinese help; the Sino-Soviet conflict (border clashes, March 1969) made both communist powers seek better relations with Washington; discontent in Eastern Europe (the Prague Spring, 1968; Polish unrest, 1970) and the cost of the arms race encouraged Soviet stability; the USSR needed Western grain and technology (large US grain purchases in 1972). West German Ostpolitik under Brandt also eased tension in Europe.

Impact in the 1970s: arms control — the Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), SALT I (1972: the ABM Treaty and an interim freeze on missile launchers), SALT II (signed 1979, never ratified by the US Senate); the Helsinki Final Act (August 1975) accepted Europe's borders but also committed signatories to human rights; cooperation such as the Apollo–Soyuz space link (1975).

Limits: arms development continued (MIRVs were not covered by SALT I); proxy wars went on; Congress linked trade to Soviet emigration policy (Jackson–Vanik, 1974); Carter's human-rights campaign angered Moscow. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 ended détente.

people.name: Mao Zedong

vocab.def: Easing of tension between the superpowers in the late 1960s–1970s.
Mutually Assured Destruction — neither side could survive a nuclear war.
Conflict in which superpowers back opposing local sides.

misconceptions.right: It limited some weapons; others (MIRVs) kept growing.
Proxy wars in Africa, the Middle East and Latin America continued.

mcq.q: Which was a reason for détente?
What did the Helsinki Final Act (1975) do?
options: Accepted Europe's borders and committed signatories to human rights

mcq.q: Where did Cuban troops support the MPLA?

short.q: In which year was SALT I signed?
What was the term for several warheads on one missile?

matching.title: Match the agreement to its year

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that détente improved relations.
evidence.model: SALT I (1972) limited ABMs and froze launchers; the Helsinki Final Act (1975) accepted Europe's borders; Apollo–Soyuz (1975) symbolised cooperation.

flashcards.a: Nixon and Kissinger playing the USSR and China off against each other.
Neither side could win a nuclear war, so limiting arms and managing crises was in both interests.
Yom Kippur War 1973; Angola from 1975; Ethiopia–Somalia 1977–78 (also Chile 1973).
Vietnam; Sino-Soviet conflict; discontent in Eastern Europe; Soviet need for grain imports (plus cost of arms).
Proxy wars, continued arms build-up, human-rights disputes, SALT II not ratified, Afghanistan 1979.

checklist.text: I can explain the role of Brezhnev, Gromyko, Mao, Nixon and Kissinger and the impact of summits.
I can explain the balance of terror and MAD.
I can describe proxy wars in Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.
I can judge the reasons for and impact of détente in the 1970s.
